supplementalTalkingPoints.label: Optional: Mention Questrade's MCP strategy.
supplementalTalkingPoints.content:
One other thing that caught my attention was Questrade's move into agentic finance. I saw that you've introduced an MCP integration that lets customers connect tools like Claude and ChatGPT to their brokerage accounts.

I thought that was interesting because you're not trying to force customers into another AI interface. You're letting them use tools they're already familiar with, while maintaining control over access to their accounts and requiring approval for trades.

I've been experimenting quite a bit with AI-assisted development and agent workflows myself, so it's a direction I'm genuinely interested in.

It also made me curious about how that thinking might eventually extend into everyday banking, where trust, data accuracy and permission boundaries become even more important.

I'd anchor on why existing investors might adopt Questbank as a primary relationship — recurring deposits, transactional activity and retained balances — not just opening another account. Publicly, Questbank has moved toward regulated everyday banking with partners like Temenos for core capabilities. My job would be to translate that ambition into sequenced customer value, reliability and economics without pretending brokerage trust automatically transfers.

How would you design MCP or agentic fina.spokenAnswer: I'd start from customer-controlled consent: OAuth-style authorization, least privilege, read-only by default, and clear listing of what an agent can see versus do. Draft insights and proposed actions should be separable from execution — especially trades, transfers or bill payments. Questrade's public MCP materials emphasize customer approval for trades; I'd extend that pattern to any material money movement. Logging, revocation, rate limits and error surfaces matter as much as the demo. I would not describe autonomous agents moving money without an explicit confirmation step and audit trail.
